did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a double call: “Awake, awake!” Zion is called to rise, put on strength and splendid garments, and return to her status as the “holy city.”

Did you know? Jerusalem is portrayed as sitting in the dust, and the prophet calls her to rise and shake it off. At the same time, she is commanded to free herself from the bonds around her neck, symbolizing release from oppression.
Did you know? Redemption is described in terms of contrast: “You were sold for nothing”—the people were sold without receiving payment, and therefore they will also be redeemed “not with money.”
Did you know? The passage mentions Egypt and Assyria in connection with Israel’s history: Egypt, where the people went to live, and Assyria, which oppressed them without cause.

Did you know? According to the chapter, the process of redemption will lead the people to recognize the name of the Lord: “Therefore my people shall know my name.” Immediately afterward comes the declaration, “Here I am.”
Did you know? The messenger of redemption is described as announcing peace, goodness, and salvation. The climax of his message is the declaration: “Your God reigns!”
Did you know? Jerusalem’s watchmen are described as raising their voices and singing together because they see “eye to eye” the Lord’s return to Zion.
Did you know? Redemption is not presented as a hidden event alone: the Lord bares his “holy arm” before all the nations, and all the ends of the earth see the salvation of Israel’s God.

Did you know? Those leaving exile are commanded to purify themselves and not touch anything unclean, because they carry the vessels of the Lord. Their departure is therefore also connected with spiritual responsibility.
Did you know? Unlike a hurried departure, the one described here is not made in panic: the Lord goes before the people, and the God of Israel gathers them from behind.
Did you know? The final section presents “my servant” as one who will succeed, be exalted, lifted up, and greatly raised—a sequence of verbs emphasizing his remarkable rise.
Did you know? The chapter creates a sharp contrast between the servant’s former condition, whose appearance and form were disfigured in the eyes of many, and the exaltation described afterward.
Did you know? At the end, many nations and kings respond with astonishment: they see and consider something that had not been told to them and that they had never heard before.
